question: To which tradition does the Tirukkuṟaḷ belong — Jain, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, or none?

sides.position: The Kuṟaḷ is a Jain work, its author identified by Jain tradition with Elācārya (Kundakunda).
arguments: The ethics of non-killing and abstention from meat (chapters 26, 33) are central, above sacrifice (259).

'He who walked upon the flower' (3) is the Jina, who walks on golden lotuses; 'the one of eight qualities' (9) is the liberated Siddha with eight qualities; 'the ocean/wheel of virtue' (8) is the Jina of the dharma-wheel.
No Vedic deity or ritual is endorsed; the Jain commentator of the Nīlakēci cites the Kuṟaḷ as 'our scripture' (moderate confidence).

sides.position: The Kuṟaḷ is Śaiva: Tiruvaḷḷuvar is honoured as a Nāyaṉār; its God of eight qualities is Śiva with the eight attributes of the Āgamas; its 'two deeds' and 'feet of the Lord' are Śaiva teaching; Śaiva authors (Umāpati's Tiruvaruṭpayaṉ) follow its form.
arguments: Parimēlaḻakar glosses eṇkuṇattāṉ with Śiva's eight Āgamic qualities.
Kuṟaḷ 5 speaks of the two deeds (iruviṉai) as Tamil Siddhānta does.

sides.position: The Kuṟaḷ belongs to the Vedic-Vaiṣṇava world: it alludes to the one who measured the worlds with his feet (610) and the world of the lotus-eyed one (1103); its three books follow dharma, artha and kāma, as the Vaiṣṇava commentator Parimēlaḻakar reads it.

A Buddhist reading (notably by the Tamil Buddhist revivalist Iyothee Thass, recent) takes the Lord of the first chapter as the Buddha, walker on lotuses and turner of the dharma-wheel, and the ethics as Buddhist.
arguments: The lineage id is approximate: the claim is modern and not tied to a specific Buddhist school.

sides.position: Non-sectarian reading (much modern Tamil scholarship): the Kuṟaḷ names no sectarian god and is 'the common scripture' (potumaṟai) for all; each tradition reads its own deity into epithets the author chose to leave open.
arguments: The first chapter's epithets are generic; no sect's rites are prescribed.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: authorship is a historical question no principle settles; the ethical teachings are shared by all claimants.
reconciliation.detail: Under P2 each tradition reads the unnamed Lord of chapter 1 from its own standpoint, and all accept the ethics; this does not decide the author's affiliation.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Jain and Śaiva claimants each hold that the epithets have one correct referent; the non-sectarian side itself rejects any single referent.

candidate_readings: Jain author (Zvelebil and others lean this way on internal evidence)
an author of the shared Tamil ethical milieu drawing on Jain and Brahmanical ideas, deliberately non-sectarian
notes: Needs an RQ id in RECONCILE_QUEUE.md (U18 cannot write outside its shard).

question: Is release won by Śiva's grace and worship, or by the Jina's path of self-discipline? (the Tamil Śaiva–Jain contests)

sides.position: Śiva alone saves by grace; the Jain monks' austerities, nakedness and denial of the Lord and the Veda are fruitless; the Lord's name, ash and temples protect the devotee.
arguments: The tenth verse of Campantar's patikams denounces Jains and Buddhists.
Appar's return from Jainism and survival of persecution by grace.

sides.position: Release is gained by right faith, knowledge and conduct, by one's own effort and austerity, without a creator's grace; non-violence is the highest dharma (position as held in Jain texts; in the Śaiva sources it is reported by opponents).
arguments: Reported here chiefly through Śaiva sources (reported by opponent).

historical_debates.name: The contest at Madurai
historical_debates.accounts: Periya Purāṇam and Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam: Campantar cured the king's fever with sacred ash; in the fire ordeal his palm-leaf hymn did not burn, in the water ordeal it floated upstream on the Vaikai; the Jains, having wagered their lives, were impaled (the tradition's account; no Jain account of the event is known, and its historicity is doubted by scholars).
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Śaiva sources: victory of Śaivism and conversion of the king.

historical_debates.name: Appar's trials under the Pallava king
historical_debates.accounts: Lime-kiln, poison, elephant and the sea; he survived by singing Śiva's names and the king (identified with Mahendravarman I) became a Śaiva.

historical_debates.name: Māṇikkavācakar's debate with the Buddhists of Laṅkā
historical_debates.accounts: At Chidambaram he defeated Buddhist teachers and made the Laṅkan king's mute daughter speak (Tiruviḷaiyāṭal and later accounts).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: a P3 reading (grace for the devotional temperament, self-discipline for the ascetic) is a candidate only.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Both the Tēvāram and Jain teaching deny that the other's path leads to release.

candidate_readings: P3-path: complementary paths for different temperaments
P4-stage: ethics shared, divergence in the ultimate

question: Is Śiva the material cause of the world, or only its efficient cause?

sides.position: Śiva is only the efficient cause; māyā (and bindu) is the material cause and his power the instrument; if Śiva were the material he would be insentient and changing and would share the world's impurity.
The same: the world arises from māyā as its material; the Lord, one with it by pervasion, is not transformed (Civañāṉa Pōtam 1 and its commentaries).
Śiva manifests the world within his own consciousness as a reflection (ābhāsa), by his freedom; he is both its material and efficient cause without loss (as recorded by U19).
Brahman is both material and efficient cause, the world being its apparent transformation (vivarta) through māyā (as recorded by U13).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled; a P2 reading (substance-standpoint realism vs absolute-standpoint non-dualism) is a candidate.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Siddhānta rejects any reading in which māyā or souls are Śiva's own substance or appearance; the non-dualists reject a second eternal reality.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: analytic realism vs absolute non-duality
P1-level: at the conventional level māyā is the material; ultimately only Śiva (rejected by the Siddhānta)

question: Does the liberated soul become identical with Śiva, or only equal to Śiva (śivasamatva) while remaining distinct?

sides.position: Sanskrit exegetes: the freed soul becomes a Śiva, equal in omniscience and omnipotence, its own powers manifested; it remains distinct and does not perform the cosmic acts; the liberations of other schools (isolation, extinction, merger) are refuted.

Tamil school: release is inseparable union (advaita as ananya) — the soul, its malas powerless, abides in Śiva enjoying his bliss, 'one, other and together'; it neither becomes Śiva nor stands as a second Lord; 'Śivasamavāda' and 'Saṅkrāntavāda' are refuted.

reconciliation.explanation: Within the Siddhānta the two sides may be complementary standpoints (analytic: the soul's manifest powers; experiential: its enjoyment in Śiva); not yet reconciled with the non-dualists.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Tamil authors reject 'equality' readings that make the soul a second agent; Sanskrit exegetes reject any merger that ends the soul's distinctness; both reject identity.

candidate_readings: P2-standpoint between Sanskrit and Tamil Siddhānta
queued against Pratyabhijñā and Advaita identity
notes: U18 contributes the Sanskrit-exegete and Tamil-school sides to U19's dispute.

question: Is the root impurity (āṇava mala) a real substance removable only by ritual initiation, or is it ignorance removed by knowledge?

sides.position: Mala is a substance (dravya); knowledge cannot remove it any more than knowing a cataract cures it; Śiva removes it through the initiation rite.
Āṇava is eternal and is never destroyed; grace makes its power ineffective, like a snake's poison stilled by a mantra; knowledge given by grace (not the soul's own effort) accompanies this.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled with the Trika; the Tamil and Sanskrit Siddhānta agree that mala is real and removed or quelled by Śiva, not by the soul's knowledge.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Siddhānta rejects the Trika's treatment of its view as a lower level.

question: Does initiation (dīkṣā) itself liberate, or is knowledge the direct cause of liberation?

sides.position: Initiation liberates, by Śiva's power working through the ācārya; knowledge alone cannot remove a substance.
Initiation by the guru (in seven modes) destroys stored karma, and knowledge of Śiva by grace brings union; both are Śiva's grace, and the jñāna-pāda is the culmination of the four.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled with the Trika position; the Tamil emphasis on jñāna is within the Siddhānta frame.

question: What occasions the descent of power (śaktipāta): the equality of karma, the maturing of impurity, or the Lord's free will alone?

sides.position: The ripening of mala (malaparipāka) is the occasion; the Lord, not the mala, is the cause.
Both: when the two deeds are balanced (iruviṉaiyoppu) and āṇava has ripened (malaparipākam), grace descends in four grades.

reconciliation.explanation: Karma-balance and mala-ripening are two descriptions of the soul's readiness (causal standpoint); the Lord's will is the agent (divine standpoint).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Trika denies that readiness conditions the Lord's free will.
